extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal historians, and practicing lawyers studying English common law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Blackstone's common-law doctrines on allegiance (express and implied; natural vs local), the legal status and rights of aliens/denizens/naturalization, and the privileges, disabilities, ranks, and appointments of the clergy under English law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between liege (feudum ligium) and simple homage
rubrics_metrics.description: Liege (feudum ligium) or liege-fee includes fealty (oath of faith) to an absolute superior and the services attendant on it; simple homage is merely an acknowledgement of tenure without the particular fealty and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereign princes did homage to each other, the species of homage (liege or simple) mattered (example: Edward III's homage to Philip VI, 1329). The text explains terminology: liege men (homines ligii), liege lord (dominus ligius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express oath of allegiance (historical forms and changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient oath of allegiance (long used) promised to be true and faithful to the king and his heirs, to bear truth and faith of life and limb and terrene honour, and to disclose and defend against intended harm; after the Revolution the form was shortened to a general promise to be faithful and bear true allegiance to the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Matthew Hale praised the older form as short, plain, and comprehensive; post-Revolution form is more general and indeterminate. Related oaths: oath of supremacy (renunciation of pope's authority) and oath of abjuration (introduced under William, recognizes the king under the Act of Settlement, renounces the pretender by name). The oath of abjuration must be taken by persons in office, trust, or employment, and may be tendered by justices to suspected persons. The oath of allegiance may be tendered to persons over age 12 in manor or sheriff's tourn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied (original/virtual) allegiance antecedent to express oath
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegiance exists as an implied, original, and virtual duty owed by every subject to the sovereign antecedently to any express oath or ceremony; the formal oath is a declaration of what the law has already imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the king's descent to sovereignty and Coke's observation that subjects are bound as if they had taken the oath 'written by the finger of the law in their hearts.' Taking an oath adds perjury if broken but does not increase the civil obligation, only unites the social and religious tie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: natural allegiance vs local (temporary) allegiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural allegiance is due from all persons born within the king's dominions immediately on birth and is perpetual; local allegiance is due from an alien for so long as he continues within the king's dominion and ceases upon departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural allegiance is a debt of gratitude, cannot be forfeited or altered except by concurrent legislature; an Englishman abroad still owes the same allegiance. Local allegiance is grounded in the implied contract of protection while resident; examples and authorities cited (e.g., Hale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-born subject cannot renounce natural allegiance by personal act
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural-born subject cannot discharge or put off natural allegiance by any act of his own (e.g., swearing to another prince); only concurrent action of the original prince (or legislature) can divest it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject voluntarily subjects himself to another sovereign he may come into conflicts of service to two masters, but his original allegiance remains unless the first prince concurs to release it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegiance applies to the sovereign's person and blood-royal (personal attachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegiance attaches not only to the regal capacity (office) but also to the sovereign's natural person and blood-royal; misapplication of allegiance to the crown alone has been punished historically (example: the Spencers under Edward II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This personal attachment supported readiness to risk life and fortune in defence of the liege lord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary allegiance to a de facto sovereign creates obligations while he is in possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an usurper is in full possession of the sovereignty, it is treason for subjects while he is in possession to act against his crown and dignity; attempts against the usurper during his possession have been punished even after the rightful sovereign regained power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Matthew Hale deduces this from the nature of local/temporary allegiance; historical example: treasons against Henry VI punished after Edward IV's restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights distinctions between natural-born subjects and aliens (time and locality criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural-born subjects possess a variety of permanent rights by birth within the king's allegiance; aliens' rights are circumscribed, acquired by residence and lost upon departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two books of the Commentaries will explain the natural-born subject's rights in detail; aliens have limited rights appropriate to their temporary connection to the realm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aliens may not acquire permanent landed property (escheat to the king)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien born abroad may purchase lands or estates but not for his own use; the king is entitled to them (escheat) on alien's attempt to acquire permanent real property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to prevent an alien from acquiring permanent allegiance and thus conflicting loyalties or foreign influence; civil law also voided such contracts. However, personal property is allowed and aliens may hire houses, trade (subject to customs duties), and bring actions for personal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aliens may own personal (movable) property and sue; droit d'aubaine contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Aliens may acquire goods, money, and other personal estate and may make wills disposing of personal estate; unlike France where _droit d'aubaine_ gave the king the alien's movable estate at death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indulgence in personal property fosters trade; aliens may trade freely but pay certain higher duties at the custom-house. Some obsolete statutes restricting alien artisans were effectively repealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of alien with certain exceptions (ambassadors, statutory children)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien is one born outside the king's dominions; exceptions include children of the king's ambassadors born abroad (treated as natural subjects) and, by statute 25 Edw. III st. 2, children born abroad whose parents were in allegiance at birth could inherit as if born in England; later statutes further extended exceptions for children whose fathers were natural-born subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern statutes (cited) have removed many restrictions so that children born abroad of English fathers are now natural-born subjects except where fathers were attainted, banished for high treason, or in service of an enemy prince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children of aliens born in England are generally natural-born subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Children born in England of alien parents are, generally speaking, natural-born subjects entitled to the same privileges as natives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with French law (jus albinatus) where children of foreign parents born on French soil remain aliens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denizen (ex donatione regis) — middle state and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A denizen is an alien born who has received letters patent of denization from the crown; he occupies a middle state between alien and natural subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denizens may take lands by purchase or devise (which aliens may not) but cannot take by inheritance. A denizen pays certain alien duties, cannot hold offices of trust (privy council, either house of parliament), or receive grants from the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalization only by Act of Parliament and statutory formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalization can be effected only by Act of Parliament, putting the alien into the same state as if born in the king's allegiance (except certain incapacities like parliamentary membership). Bills for naturalization must contain disabling clauses; naturalization or restoration in blood requires reception of the sacrament within one month before the bill and taking oaths of allegiance and supremacy before Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory citations provided (e.g., 1 Geo. I. c. 4; 7 Jac. I. c. 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory paths to naturalization and special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutory provisions naturalize specific persons: e.g., foreign seamen serving two years on an English ship are ipso facto naturalized; foreign Protestants and Jews in certain American colonies after seven years' residence and taking oaths are naturalized to the same extent as native Protestants or Jews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory naturalizations carried particular qualifications and were subject to political controversies (e.g., the Jew-bill debates and temporary enactments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy exemptions from secular duties and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Clergy (persons in holy orders and ecclesiastical offices) enjoy personal exemptions: cannot be compelled to serve on juries, attend court-leet or view of frank-pledge, be chosen to temporal offices (bailiff, reeve, constable), and during divine service are privileged from arrest in civil suits; in felony cases they may claim the benefit of clergy (without branding) and may receive it more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These privileges largely remain though some were abridged at the Reformation; case law and statutes cited. If a layman takes orders after being summoned to jury, he must still appear and be sworn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy disabilities (secular restrictions and penalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerics are subject to disabilities: cannot sit in the House of Commons; by statute 21 Hen. VIII c.13 clerks are forbidden to take lands to farm (penalty 10_l._ per month and avoidance of lease), engage in trade, or sell merchandise under forfeiture of treble value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions align with canon law and flow from the expectation of clerical dedication to sacred functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical ranks and the method of appointment (bishops and archbishops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishops and archbishops are (historically) elected by the cathedral chapter by licence from the crown, but over time the crown's right of confirmation, investiture (temporalties), and effective nomination became dominant; statutes (e.g., 25 Hen. VIII c.20) restored the crown's nomination power and set election procedures, letters patent, confirmation requirements, and penalties (praemunire) for refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical contest over investiture (per annulum et baculum vs per sceptrum) and the pope's attempts to exclude laity from elections are recounted; modern statutory form requires archbishopric or bishopric election signified to metropolitan and confirmation, investiture, consecration without recourse to Rome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archbishop's powers and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: An archbishop is chief of clergy in a province, inspects bishops and inferior clergy, may deprive on notorious cause, has a diocese and provincial jurisdiction, calls convocation on the king's writ, hears appeals from inferior jurisdictions, is guardian of spiritualties during vacancies, may present by lapse to livings, has 'option' on presentations, and (Canterbury) has privilege to crown monarchs and to grant dispensations under statute 25 Hen. VIII c.21.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some prerogatives derive from former legatine powers and imperial analogues; statutory powers to grant dispensations (not contrary to scripture) underlie licenses to marry at unusual times, hold two livings, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishop's duties and ecclesiastical jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A bishop inspects manners of people and clergy, punishes by ecclesiastical censures to effect reformation, holds visits and courts (administered by a chancellor who must be a doctor of civil law), and institutes and directs induction to ecclesiastical livings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory qualifications for chancellors (Stat. 37 Hen. VIII c.17) and description of episcopal administrative structure are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancies and resignation rules for archbishopricks and bishopricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Archbishopricks and bishopricks may become void by death, deprivation for gross and notorious crime, or resignation; resignations must be made to a superior (a bishop must resign to his metropolitan; an archbishop can resign only to the king).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority citation given; distinctions of resignee and manner of vacancy explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dean and chapter: composition, election, and relation to bishop
rubrics_metrics.description: The dean and chapter act as the bishop's council for religion and temporal concerns; deans are elected by chapter with conge d'eslire and letters missive from the king (like bishops) though some deaneries created from dissolved monasteries are donative; chapters may be appointed by king, bishop, or elected internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter are nominal electors of bishops (subject to royal licence), the bishop is their ordinary and may visit and correct them. Deaneries and prebends may be vacated by death, deprivation, or resignation to king or bishop. Historical check on bishop grants (pre-32 Hen. VIII c.28) noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archdeacon jurisdiction and courts
rubrics_metrics.description: An archdeacon holds ecclesiastical jurisdiction subordinate to the bishop across a diocese or part of it, usually appointed by the bishop, visits the clergy, and maintains a separate court for spiritual censures and other ecclesiastical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally deriving episcopal authority, the archdeacon's office is now distinct and independent in many respects (authority citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural deans as ancient deputies with inferior authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Rural deans are very ancient officers, acting as deputies of the bishop around the diocese to inspect parochial clergy and armed with an inferior degree of judicial and coercive authority; though almost grown out of use, the deaneries may still subsist as ecclesiastical divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical origin and diminished modern role noted; references cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parson (persona ecclesiae): legal character and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A parson (persona ecclesiae) has full possession of all rights of a parochial church, represents the church corporeally, is a body corporate with perpetual succession, and holds freehold in parsonage house, glebe, tithes, and other dues; benefices may be appropriated to spiritual corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the historical tithe division into parts (bishop, fabrick, poor, incumbent) and how appropriation by monasteries arose to apply funds to their corporations subject to burthen of church repairs and supply. The parson's legal dignity and succession are emphasized.
